title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{t:forT} 
Let $T^*$ be any fixed regular tournament with at least three vertices. Then 
$f_n\sim\hat f_n$ and
$$
{\bf E} [H({\cal T}(T^*))]\sim f_ng(dn)\left( \frac{2}{d}\right)^{dn}(2\pi
n)^{(d-1)/2}\frac{d^{3/2}}{d-1}.
$$
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{t:coeff} 
 Provided ${\cal H}\ne 0$,  
$$
{\bf E} [H({\cal T}(T^*))]  \sim    
g(dn)\sqrt\frac{d}{ {\cal H}}.
$$

title: Conjecture
body_md:
\label{con1}
 For all $d\ge 3$, the maximum of 
$  {\bf E} [H({\cal T}(T^*))] $, over all tournaments $T^*$ on $d$ vertices ($d$ odd,
and $n$ sufficiently large), is achieved for $T^*=R_d$.

title: Conjecture
body_md:
For every regular tournament $T^*$ on at least three vertices,
${\cal H}\ne 0$ and $d/{\cal H}$ is the square of a rational.

title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
A
Hamilton cycle in
$Q$ projects onto a closed walk $W$ in $T^*$ (by mapping $T_i$ to the vertex
$i$ and ignoring loops). Let
$j_i$  denote the number of arcs of
$W$ whose head is 
$i$ (which is of course equal to the number with tail  $i$).  
Distinguish a special ``initial" vertex $v$ in $T_1$ such that the arc
$wv$ of $Q$ has $w\notin V(T_1)$. This introduces a multiplicity of $j_1$
into the counting. For each $i$, the
arcs of  $Q$ induce an ordered spanning forest $F_i$  of $T_i$, i.e.\ a
set of
$j_i$ disjoint directed paths (perhaps some containing only one vertex)
which cover the vertices of
$T_i$, the ordering determined by the initial vertex $v$. The number of
such spanning forests which can ever appear is $n!\left(n-1\atop
j_i-1\right)$, since they can be formed from a Hamilton path on $V(T_i)$
by deleting
$j_i-1$ edges. Any such spanning forest $F_i$ contains
$n-j_i$ arcs, so the probability that
$T_i$ contains $F_i$ is
$2^{-n+j_i}$. Moreover since the
$T_i$ are independent, the probability that they   contain a given set of
forests $F_1,\ldots, F_d$ is
$\prod_i 2^{-n+j_i}$. Given these forests and, in addition, the walk
$W$, we can reconstruct the original Hamilton cycle in 
$Q$. The number of closed walks
$W$   starting
at vertex 1, and with parameters $j_i$ as above, is
$[x_1^{j_1}\cdots x_d^{j_d}] f(x_1,\ldots ,x_d)$,  with $f(x_1,\ldots,
x_d)$ defined as before. The  lemma now follows by
linearity of expectation (and dividing by $j_1$ to ignore the choice of
$v$). ~~\vrule height8pt width4pt depth0pt
head: manual

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{final}
If $T^*$ is regular then, in the summation in~(\ref{first}), $(1-o(1))$ of the
contribution comes from terms with $j_i=(1+o(1))(d-1)n/d$ for all $i$.
In particular,
$$
{\bf E} [H({\cal T}(T^*))] \sim  \frac{d (n!2^{-n})^d}{(d-1)n}\sum_{j_1,\ldots , j_d\ge
1}  [x_1^{j_1}\cdots x_d^{j_d}] f(x_1,\ldots ,x_d)
\prod_{i=1}^d  \left(n-1\atop j_i-1\right) 2^{j_i}.
$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Consider restricting the summation in~(\ref{first}) to
those parameters such that $\sum_i j_i = dj$ for some fixed $j$.
Since the out-degree of each vertex in
$T^*$ is $(d-1)/2$, there are $((d-1)/2)^{dj}$ walks of length $dj$, and
moreover  the position of a random walker will
converge to the uniform distribution. Thus, the sum of all the
coefficients of
$f$ in~(\ref{first}) with $\sum_i j_i = dj$ is asymptotic to
$((d-1)/2)^{dj}/d$, and almost all of the value is contributed by the
terms with $|j_i-j|<\epsilon j/2d$ ($1\le j \le d$) for any fixed $\epsilon>0$.   
By making use of the
log-concavity of the factors in the product in~(\ref{first}), it is
straightforward to show that for the above-mentioned terms, this product is at
least as large as it is if $|j_i-j|>\epsilon j$ for any $i$. Hence terms of the
latter type contribute negligibly to the summation. For the other
(non-negligible) terms, Stirling's formula shows that the product has value
\begin{equation}\label{factor}
\frac{n^{dn}2^{dj} \exp(\Theta(\epsilon^2 n))}{j^{dj}(n-j)^{d(n-j)}}.
\end{equation}
 
On the other hand, the product of this
with the sum of coefficients, $((d-1)/2)^{dj}/d$,  is easily seen to be
maximised for $j\sim (d-1)n/d$ (apart from the error term), and it is easy
to see that unless $|j-(d-1)n/d|=O(\epsilon)$ the
contribution will be negligible.  The
lemma follows (on taking $\epsilon \to 0$ slowly). ~~\vrule height8pt width4pt depth0pt

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{paths}
For each $n\ge 1$ let $F_n$ be either a directed graph on $n$ labelled
vertices with each component a directed path, or a directed Hamilton
cycle.  Then the probability that
$F_n$ appears in a random 
$n$-vertex regular tournament is asymptotically equal to
$2^{-a(F_n)}e^{a(F_n)/n-s(F_n)/n}$ as $n\to\infty$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Following~\cite{M}, the number of regular tournaments on
$n$ vertices is precisely
\begin{equation}\label{countx}
 RT(n)={1\over (2\pi i)^n}\oint\cdots\oint
  { \prod_{1\le j<k\le n}(x_j^{-1}x_k+x_jx_k^{-1})\over
x_1x_2\cdots x_n  }\,
  dx_1dx_2\cdots dx_n,
\end{equation}
where each integral is around the circle $|z|=1$ in the anticlockwise
direction. The numerator of the integrand is the generating function for
tournaments enumerated by the excess of out-degree over in-degree at each
vertex. Under the substitution $x_j=e^{i\theta_j}$ this becomes
\begin{equation}\label{countth}
 RT(n)={2^{n(n-1)/2}\over (2\pi i)^n}\int_{U_n(\pi)}
   \prod_{1\le j<k\le n}\cos(\theta_j-\theta_k)\,
  d\theta_1d\theta_2\cdots d\theta_n 
\end{equation}
where $U_n(x)$ denotes $[-x,x]^n$.
For the general situation it suffices to consider the
case that $F_n$ is a subdigraph of the directed path $1,2,\ldots ,n$, with
the ordering imposed on the paths components being the natural one. (The
Hamilton cycle case requires only a trivial modification to the argument
for the case $a(F)=n-1$, and we make no further remark on it.) Then  all
arcs of $F_n$ are of the form
$(j,j+1)$. Let $E=\{j:(j,j+1)\in E(F)\}$.  Then the number $N(F_n)$ of
tournaments containing $F_n$ is expressed as an integral
like~(\ref{countx}), but with the following factors altered:   if
$j\in E$ and $k=j+1$, the factor $(x_j^{-1}x_k+x_jx_k^{-1})$ is replaced
by $x_jx_k^{-1}$. This means that the expression in~(\ref{countth}) for the
current problem becomes
\begin{equation}\label{adjustth}
 N(F_n) = {2^{n(n-1)/2-a(F_n)}\over (2\pi i)^n}\int_{U_n(\pi)}
  \frac{ \prod_{1\le j<k\le n}\cos(\theta_j-\theta_k)}{ \prod_{j\in
E}\cos(\theta_j-\theta_{j+1})}
\,\frac{\prod_{j\in E^+} e^{i\theta_j}}{ \prod_{j\in E^-}  e^{i\theta_j}}\,
  d\theta_1d\theta_2\cdots d\theta_n
\end{equation}
where $E^+$ ($E^-$) is the set of vertices which begin (end) a directed
path. Thus $E^+=\{j:(j,j+1)\in E(F), (j-1,j)\notin E(F)\}$, and for
defining
$E^-$, switch $\in$ and $\notin$.  


We continue to follow the argument in~\cite{M} and split the integral
in~(\ref{adjustth}) into three
major parts. For some $\epsilon>0$, let $I_1$ denote the contribution
coming from those points at which
$|\theta_j-\theta_n|\le n^{-1/2+\epsilon/4}$ or $|\theta_j-\theta_n+\pi|\le
n^{-1/2+\epsilon/4}$ for $1\le j \le n-1$, where $\theta_j$ values are mod
$2\pi$. Still valid in the present context is the argument in~\cite{M}
that we may set $\theta_n=0$ and assume all the $\theta_j$ are clustered near
0, which in this case gives
\begin{equation}\label{eye1}
I_1 = 2^n\pi
 \int_{U_{n-1}(n^{-1/2+\epsilon/4})}
  \frac{ \prod_{1\le j<k\le n}\cos(\theta_j-\theta_k)}{ \prod_{j\in
E}\cos(\theta_j-\theta_{j+1})}\,
\frac{\prod_{j\in E^+} e^{i\theta_j}}{ \prod_{j\in E^-}  e^{i\theta_j}}\,
  d \theta_1d\theta_2\cdots d\theta_{n-1}.
\end{equation}
Expanding (most of) the integrand gives (dropping terms dominated by the
$o(1)$ error term),
\begin{eqnarray}&&\exp\left(o(1)+\sum_{1\le j<k\le n} -\frac12
(\theta_j-\theta_k)^2-\frac{1}{12}(\theta_j-\theta_k)^4\right)\label{line1}\\
&&\times 
\exp\left(\sum_{j\in E^+}  {i\theta_j}\, +
\sum_{j\in E^-}  {-i\theta_j}
 \, +
\sum_{j\in E}  \frac12 (\theta_j-\theta_{j+1})^2  
\right),\label{line2}
\end{eqnarray}
where the first line contains the terms in the original
calculation in ~\cite{M}.

The next step is to apply the linear transformation 
$$y_j=\theta_j-\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\theta_k/(n+\sqrt n),$$
for $1\le j\le n-1$, which implies using~\cite[Equation (2)]{M} that
$\theta_j=y_j+\phi$ where 
$$\phi = \sum_{k=1}^{n-1} y_k/(1+\sqrt n).$$
The transformed logarithm of~(\ref{line1})  is dealt with in~\cite{M},
the significant terms being 
~\begin{equation}\label{old}
-\frac{n}{2} \sum_{k=1}^{n-1} y_k^2
-\frac{n}{12} \sum_{k=1}^{n-1} y_k^4-\frac{n}{4} (\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}
y_k^2)^2.
\end{equation}
For the
logarithm of~(\ref{line2}), note that $|E^+|=|E^-|$ and so every $\phi$
which might appear is actually cancelled out. This gives
\begin{equation}\label{newterms} \sum_{j\in E^+} iy_j \,+
\sum_{j\in E^-} -iy_j 
\,+\sum_{j\in E}  \frac12 (y_j-y_{j+1})^2.
\end{equation}
However, $y_n$ (if it appears) must be defined as $-\phi$, which is a
function of the other $y_j$. To handle the integral (of the exponential of
all these terms) we may use the averaging argument leading to~\cite[Equation
(2.4)]{MW}. This converts these terms into
$$ \sum_{j\in E^+} - y_j^2\, +
\sum_{j\in E}  \frac12 (y_j^2 +y_{j+1}^2) +o(1). 
$$
(The effect of the terms $iy_j$ can be gauged by considering the effect
of $J$ in the proof of~\cite[Lemma~3]{MW}. The terms involving $y_n$, if
they appear, similarly have negligible affect on the result of the
averaging. The only different type of term this might produce appears if
$n-1\in E$, so that $y_n^2$ appears. A term like the fourth power of $y_n$
appears in~\cite[Lemma~3]{MW} with coefficient $I$, and has negligible
effect.) To evaluate~(\ref{eye1}) we must integrate the exponential of the sum
of this and~(\ref{old}). The result is easily seen to be 
$W\exp(-|E^+|/n+|E|/n) = W\exp(a(F_n)/n-s(F_n)/n)$ where
$W=(2\pi/n)^{(n-1)/2}\sqrt{n/e}$ is the original integral due to
the terms in~(\ref{old}). Note that together with the extra factors
outside the integral in~(\ref{adjustth}) as compared to~(\ref{countth}), this
gives the result desired for the theorem.

It remains only to show that the part of the integral outside
$I_1$ is negligible. The factors $e^{i\theta_j}$
in~(\ref{eye1}) have absolute value 1 so can be ignored. For the rest, the
argument from~\cite{M} needs to be modified in a few small ways to be able
to cope with the extra factor $\prod_{j\in
E}\cos(\theta_j-\theta_{j+1})^{-1}$. We now refer heavily to the argument
in~\cite{M}, which splits the remaining part of the integral up into
pieces denoted $I_2(r)$ and $I_3(h)$. At the point where values
$\theta_j$ satisfying
$|\theta_j|<\pi/8$ are singled out for evaluating $I_2(r)$, one may instead
consider
$|\theta_j|<1/\eta$  for a sufficiently small  
$\eta>0$. Then the value of $\prod_{j\in E}\cos(\theta_j-\theta_{j+1})^{-1}$ can
be made sufficiently small that it is dominated by the
exponentially small bound obtained on $I_2(r)$. For $I_3(h)$, a similar
modification is required: by  considering, in addition to what is already
in~\cite{M}, the number
$h'$ of $\theta_j$ satisfying $n^{-1/2+\eta\epsilon}\le |\theta_j|\le
n^{-1/2+\epsilon/4}$, this case is also seen to be negligible. The
lemma follows. ~~\vrule height8pt width4pt depth0pt

title: Theorem
body_md:
\cite{PW} \label{t:PW}
With the assumptions and definitions in the paragraph above, if $G({\bf z})\ne 0$ and
${\cal H}\ne 0$ then for
${\bf r}\in\mbox{dir}({\bf z})$
$$[y_1^{r_1}\cdots y_d^{r_d}]\,\frac{G({\bf y})}{K({\bf y})}
\sim
(2\pi)^{(1-d)/2}\frac{G({\bf z})}{-z_dK_d({\bf z})\sqrt{{\cal H}}}\prod_{j=1}^dz_j^{-r_j}.$$
